summary:
The Kids Online Safety and Privacy Act primarily establishes federal duties for covered online services used by minors and expands the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act of 1998 (“COPPA”), while also revising federal reporting-sunset procedures.

Title I, subtitle A (“Kids Online Safety”), creates a freestanding regulatory regime for “covered platforms” used or reasonably likely to be used by minors under 17, excluding specified carriers, broadband, email, conferencing, nonprofit, educational, library, news/sports, business software, VPN, and related services (§101). Section 102 imposes a duty of reasonable care in creating and implementing design features to prevent and mitigate specified harms to minors, including enumerated mental health disorders, addiction-like use, violence/bullying/harassment, sexual exploitation and abuse, marketing of narcotics, tobacco, gambling, or alcohol, and financial harms, without requiring platforms to block deliberate searches or access to prevention resources. Section 103 requires minor safeguards, default protective settings, parental tools, reporting mechanisms with response deadlines, and prohibits facilitating advertisements for specified illegal or age-restricted products to known minors; it includes dark-pattern, gameplay, third-party control, and construction provisions. Sections 104 and 105 require notices, recommendation-system disclosures, ad labeling, parental/minor resources, and annual public risk/audit reports for large user-generated-content platforms. Sections 106–109 direct FTC/National Academy studies, market-research guidance, an age-verification study by Commerce/FCC/FTC, and FTC guidance. Section 110 makes violations enforceable by the FTC as violations of rules under FTC Act §18(a)(1)(B), 15 U.S.C. 57a(a)(1)(B), and authorizes State attorneys general to enforce §§103–105 subject to notice, intervention, and pendency limitations; State AGs may not base State-law liability on §102. Section 111 establishes a Kids Online Safety Council exempt from FACA. Subtitle A generally takes effect 18 months after enactment (§112) and includes nonpreemption of FERPA, COPPA, FTC Act §18(h), and Communications Act §230; it does not require age collection, age gating, or age verification (§113).

Title I, subtitle B requires, one year after enactment, online platforms using “opaque algorithms” to provide specified notices and allow users to switch to an “input-transparent algorithm,” without differential pricing; violations are FTC-enforceable (§§120–121). Subtitle C provides conflict preemption only, preserves more protective State laws, and includes severability (§§130–131).

Title II amends COPPA, 15 U.S.C. 6501–6505, to cover teens ages 13–16, online and mobile applications, expanded “personal information,” geolocation, connected devices, and “individual-specific advertising to children or teens” (§201). It prohibits covered operators with actual or fairly implied knowledge from collecting, using, disclosing, maintaining, retaining, or transferring children’s or teens’ personal information in specified ways, including individual-specific advertising, unnecessary collection, foreign storage/transfer without direct notice, and excessive retention; expands notice, verifiable-consent, access, deletion, correction, security, educational-agreement, safe-harbor publication, State-enforcement, and banking-enforcement provisions; and requires FTC guidance within 180 days and a common-consent feasibility report within one year. Sections 202 and 203 require FTC reports on application-platform oversight and COPPA enforcement and a GAO study on teen fintech privacy. Section 204 provides severability.

Title III amends 31 U.S.C. 1125 to require agencies to include in budget justification materials lists of recurring congressional plans or reports, identify outdated or duplicative reports, and recommend sunset, modification, consolidation, or reduced frequency, with citations, committee lists, and justifications; it preserves underlying submission duties. It repeals 31 U.S.C. 1105(a)(39) and amends §§7244(a)–(b) of the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023 to conform electronic submission and OMB guidance requirements (§301).
